analysis.one_liner: Charges large electricity-using facilities for their annual power use under the Clean Air Act.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in September 2026 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where no action has been taken and no vote has been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: Representative Paul Tonko introduced a bill to amend the Clean Air Act so the Environmental Protection Agency must impose and collect a charge on the total annual electricity consumed by certain large facilities, paid by the facilities' owners or operators. The idea is to make heavy power users pay for their electricity footprint, giving them a financial reason to use less. The bill was sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the public would benefit through a charge that pushes large electricity consumers to use less power, and the EPA would collect payments from the covered facilities' owners or operators.

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires the EPA to impose and collect a charge on the total annual electricity consumption of certain facilities, billed to the facilities' owners or operators [S1].
A charge on heavy electricity use gives covered facilities a direct financial reason to reduce their power consumption [S1].

analysis.who_pays: The owners or operators of the covered facilities would pay the charge on their annual electricity consumption.

drawbacks.text: The bill, as described on its face, imposes a charge on owners or operators of covered facilities, and businesses facing a per-consumption charge generally have an incentive to pass added costs along to customers through higher prices [S1].
The bill has no cosponsors, so it carries no visible coalition of support even within its sponsor's own party [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A charge on heavy electricity users could reduce consumption and make large power consumers bear their footprint's cost. The tradeoff is that facilities may pass the charge to customers, and the bill's short title does not detail which facilities are covered, how the charge is set, or what happens to the money collected. With no cosponsors and no committee action, there is no record of any deliberation on these design questions.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in mid-September 2026, sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and has sat there with no hearing, no vote, and no sign of movement since.

narrative.text: Representative Paul Tonko introduced the bill in the House on September 16, 2026 [S1].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, the committee with jurisdiction over the Clean Air Act [S3].
No cosponsors have joined the bill [S2].
No further action — no markup, no floor vote, no scheduling — has been recorded [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has had to act: the large electricity consumers who would pay the charge have avoided it simply because the bill has not moved, and its sponsor has gained nothing from the referral.

for.name: Rep. Paul Tonko
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have been held and no one besides the Democratic sponsor has signed on, so the partisan shape of any future support or opposition is unknown.

industries.note: If enacted, these facilities would owe the EPA a charge on their total annual electricity consumption, raising their operating costs and giving them a reason to cut usage. Their interest in the bill runs against the public purpose of the charge.

analysis.trajectory: The bill is unlikely to advance. It was introduced roughly three and a half months before the session ends, has zero cosponsors, and has seen no committee action; the overwhelming majority of bills referred to committee die without a hearing or vote, and this one shows none of the support that would change that.
